interactions: Amiodarone + phenytoin or fosphenytoin: amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 and raises phenytoin levels; toxicity; lower doses and level monitoring if used
Fosphenytoin loading + amiodarone + metoprolol: additive cardiac depression; hypotension, bradycardia and AV block during the infusion; continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring, slower rate
Amiodarone + lacosamide: additive PR prolongation; AV block, especially with metoprolol; baseline and repeat ECG
Amiodarone + levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic or conduction interaction
Amiodarone + valproate: no relevant pharmacokinetic or conduction interaction; both can raise transaminases; monitor liver tests
Propofol + amiodarone or metoprolol: additive hypotension and bradycardia
Propofol + lorazepam or other ASMs: additive sedation and respiratory depression; no pharmacokinetic interaction
Amiodarone + atorvastatin: CYP3A4 inhibition raises atorvastatin exposure; myopathy risk; review the statin dose
Amiodarone + metoprolol: additive bradycardia and AV block

output.summary: Amiodarone raises phenytoin levels via CYP2C9, and fosphenytoin loading with amiodarone and metoprolol risks hypotension, bradycardia and AV block. Lacosamide adds PR prolongation. Levetiracetam and valproate have no conduction interaction. Propofol adds hypotension and sedation.

output.query: post-anoxic myoclonus and status epilepticus after cardiac arrest: treatment and prognostication

results.key_finding: Neuroprognostication in patients who remain comatose after cardiac arrest is multimodal and is done no earlier than 72 hours after return of circulation, once sedation and other confounders are excluded. Predictors of poor outcome include bilaterally absent N20 responses, a highly malignant EEG, high neuron-specific enolase at 48 or 72 hours, status myoclonus within 72 hours, and diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI.
results.title: European Resuscitation Council and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines 2021: post-resuscitation care

output.summary: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest combines clinical examination, electrophysiology, biomarkers and imaging, no earlier than 72 hours after return of circulation and after sedation is cleared [ERC_ESICM_2021]. No single predictor, myoclonus included, is used alone. Early post-anoxic myoclonus with a continuous reactive EEG background can be compatible with recovery. Continuous EEG is used during anaesthetic infusion and its weaning [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium normal; glucose 168 mg/dL; ALT 98 and AST 142 U/L; creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; troponin I 12.8 ng/mL; lactate 2.6 mmol/L
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; potassium and magnesium also matter with a prolonged QTc on amiodarone [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse sulcal effacement and reduced grey-white differentiation; no hemorrhage
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012]; diffuse edema on CT is also one of the post-arrest predictors [ERC_ESICM_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Burst-suppression with near-identical left-predominant epileptiform bursts; right arm and facial myoclonus time-locked to the bursts; no background reactivity
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm the electroclinical pattern of the jerks and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Periodic jerks in a comatose post-arrest patient need EEG to show whether they are time-locked to epileptiform activity; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours and during sedation weaning [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus bradycardia 58/min, QTc 498 ms, PR 168 ms, QRS 96 ms
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG with QTc and PR before choosing an antiseizure drug
action_criteria.rationale: On amiodarone and metoprolol after a VF arrest, the conduction intervals decide which second-line ASM can be loaded safely [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cortical N20 absent on both sides; N9 and N13 present
action_criteria.label: Median nerve SSEP as one modality of multimodal neuroprognostication
action_criteria.rationale: N20 responses are little affected by sedation and can be recorded from 24 hours after return of circulation; bilateral absence is one predictor of poor outcome, interpreted with the others no earlier than 72 hours [ERC_ESICM_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse cortical ribbon and bilateral putaminal and thalamic restricted diffusion
action_criteria.label: MRI brain with diffusion to define the extent of hypoxic-ischaemic injury
action_criteria.rationale: Diffuse cortical and deep grey restricted diffusion is one of the imaging predictors in multimodal post-arrest prognostication [ERC_ESICM_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CYP2C9 inhibition by amiodarone raising phenytoin; fosphenytoin hypotension, bradycardia and AV block risk; lacosamide PR effect; no conduction interaction for levetiracetam
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check: amiodarone, metoprolol and propofol against the antiseizure options
action_criteria.rationale: Amiodarone raises phenytoin levels and, with metoprolol, makes fosphenytoin loading hazardous; lacosamide adds PR prolongation; the check decides the second-line ASM [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on timing and modalities of post-arrest prognostication
action_criteria.label: Literature: post-anoxic myoclonus and post-arrest neuroprognostication
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step [ERC_ESICM_2021].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not withdraw life-sustaining treatment or give a poor prognosis before 72 hours after return of circulation and clearance of sedation, or on myoclonus or any single predictor alone [ERC_ESICM_2021].
Do not load fosphenytoin or phenytoin on amiodarone and metoprolol: amiodarone raises phenytoin levels and loading adds hypotension, bradycardia and AV block.
Do not add QT-prolonging drugs with a QTc of 498 ms on amiodarone.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once) [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg), or valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3000 mg) as the alternative, and avoid fosphenytoin because amiodarone raises phenytoin levels and loading with amiodarone and metoprolol risks hypotension, bradycardia and AV block; avoid lacosamide because of additive PR prolongation [ESETT_2019].
Wean propofol under continuous video-EEG to separate sedation from the anoxic pattern, and continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012].
Continue temperature control at 36 C and prevent fever for at least 72 hours after return of circulation [ERC_ESICM_2021].

Defer neuroprognostication to at least 72 hours after return of circulation with sedation cleared, and make it multimodal: examination, SSEP, EEG, NSE at 48 and 72 hours, and CT or MRI; status myoclonus is one predictor and never decides alone [ERC_ESICM_2021].
Monitor QTc and rhythm on telemetry with amiodarone, keep potassium and magnesium in range, and avoid adding QT-prolonging drugs.

Ask cardiology to define the cause of the VF arrest (coronary angiography, secondary-prevention ICD), and hold a multidisciplinary meeting with his wife before any decision on life-sustaining treatment.

Carotid duplex does not bear on a global hypoxic-ischaemic injury after cardiac arrest.

patient.history_present_illness: A 62-year-old retired firefighter collapsed at a gym in a witnessed cardiac arrest. Bystanders started CPR immediately. EMS arrived 7 minutes after collapse and found ventricular fibrillation; two shocks restored spontaneous circulation about 11 minutes after collapse. He was intubated, amiodarone was started in the emergency department (150 mg IV bolus, then 1 mg/min), and he was admitted to the ICU for targeted temperature management at 36 C with propofol 10 mcg/kg/min for sedation. About 24 hours after return of spontaneous circulation, nursing noticed periodic flexion jerks of the right arm every 15 to 20 seconds with twitching of the right side of the face, and neurology was asked to see him. He has not received a benzodiazepine or an antiseizure drug. His wife reports a syncopal episode 2 weeks ago that was evaluated and called benign. He takes metoprolol, aspirin and atorvastatin for coronary artery disease. No prior epilepsy.
